# Tips and workarounds

## Cache segment restore timeout

A cache gets downloaded in multiple segments of fixed sizes (`1GB` for a `32-bit` runner and `2GB` for a `64-bit` runner). Sometimes, a segment download gets stuck which causes the workflow job to be stuck forever and fail. Version `v3.0.8` of `actions/cache` introduces a segment download timeout. The segment download timeout will allow the segment download to get aborted and hence allow the job to proceed with a cache miss.

Default value of this timeout is 10 minutes and can be customized by specifying an [environment variable](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/environment-variables) named `SEGMENT_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT_MINS` with timeout value in minutes.

## Update a cache

A cache today is immutable and cannot be updated. But some use cases require the cache to be saved even though there was a "hit" during restore. To do so, use a `key` which is unique for every run and use `restore-keys` to restore the nearest cache. For example:

  ```yaml
      - name: update cache on every commit
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: prime-numbers
          key: primes-${{ runner.os }}-${{ github.run_id }} # Can use time based key as well
          restore-keys: |
            primes-${{ runner.os }}
  ```

  Please note that this will create a new cache on every run and hence will consume the cache [quota](./README.md#cache-limits).

## Use cache across feature branches

Reusing cache across feature branches is not allowed today to provide cache [isolation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/caching-dependencies-to-speed-up-workflows#restrictions-for-accessing-a-cache). However if both feature branches are from the default branch, a good way to achieve this is to ensure that the default branch has a cache. This cache will then be consumable by both feature branches.

## Cross OS cache

From `v3.2.3` cache is cross-os compatible when `enableCrossOsArchive` input is passed as true. This means that a cache created on `ubuntu-latest` or `mac-latest` can be used by `windows-latest` and vice versa, provided the workflow which runs on `windows-latest` have input `enableCrossOsArchive` as true. This is useful to cache dependencies which are independent of the runner platform. This will help reduce the consumption of the cache quota and help build for multiple platforms from the same cache. Things to keep in mind while using this feature:

- Only cache files that are compatible across OSs.
- Caching symlinks might cause issues while restoring them as they behave differently on different OSs.
- Be mindful when caching files from outside your github workspace directory as the directory is located at different places across OS.
- Avoid using directory pointers such as `${{ github.workspace }}` or `~` (home) which eventually evaluate to an absolute path that does not match across OSs.

## Force deletion of caches overriding default cache eviction policy

Caches have [branch scope restriction](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/caching-dependencies-to-speed-up-workflows#restrictions-for-accessing-a-cache) in place. This means that if caches for a specific branch are using a lot of storage quota, it may result into more frequently used caches from `default` branch getting thrashed. For example, if there are many pull requests happening on a repo and are creating caches, these cannot be used in default branch scope but will still occupy a lot of space till they get cleaned up by [eviction policy](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/caching-dependencies-to-speed-up-workflows#usage-limits-and-eviction-policy). But sometime we want to clean them up on a faster cadence so as to ensure default branch is not thrashing.

<details>
  <summary>Example</summary>

```yaml
name: cleanup caches by a branch
on:
  pull_request:
    types:
      - closed
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  cleanup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      # `actions:write` permission is required to delete caches
      #   See also: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/cache?apiVersion=2022-11-28#delete-a-github-actions-cache-for-a-repository-using-a-cache-id
      actions: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Cleanup
        run: |
          echo "Fetching list of cache key"
          cacheKeysForPR=$(gh cache list --ref $BRANCH --limit 100 --json id --jq '.[].id')

          ## Setting this to not fail the workflow while deleting cache keys.
          set +e
          echo "Deleting caches..."
          for cacheKey in $cacheKeysForPR
          do
              gh cache delete $cacheKey
          done
          echo "Done"
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          BRANCH: refs/pull/${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}/merge
```

</details>

# Tips and workarounds

## Cache segment restore timeout

A cache gets downloaded in multiple segments of fixed sizes (`1GB` for a `32-bit` runner and `2GB` for a `64-bit` runner). Sometimes, a segment download gets stuck which causes the workflow job to be stuck forever and fail. Version `v3.0.8` of `actions/cache` introduces a segment download timeout. The segment download timeout will allow the segment download to get aborted and hence allow the job to proceed with a cache miss.

Default value of this timeout is 10 minutes and can be customized by specifying an [environment variable](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/environment-variables) named `SEGMENT_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT_MINS` with timeout value in minutes.

## Update a cache

A cache today is immutable and cannot be updated. But some use cases require the cache to be saved even though there was a "hit" during restore. To do so, use a `key` which is unique for every run and use `restore-keys` to restore the nearest cache. For example:

  ```yaml
      - name: update cache on every commit
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: prime-numbers
          key: primes-${{ runner.os }}-${{ github.run_id }} # Can use time based key as well
          restore-keys: |
            primes-${{ runner.os }}
  ```

  Please note that this will create a new cache on every run and hence will consume the cache [quota](./README.md#cache-limits).

## Use cache across feature branches

Reusing cache across feature branches is not allowed today to provide cache [isolation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/caching-dependencies-to-speed-up-workflows#restrictions-for-accessing-a-cache). However if both feature branches are from the default branch, a good way to achieve this is to ensure that the default branch has a cache. This cache will then be consumable by both feature branches.

## Cross OS cache

From `v3.2.3` cache is cross-os compatible when `enableCrossOsArchive` input is passed as true. This means that a cache created on `ubuntu-latest` or `mac-latest` can be used by `windows-latest` and vice versa, provided the workflow which runs on `windows-latest` have input `enableCrossOsArchive` as true. This is useful to cache dependencies which are independent of the runner platform. This will help reduce the consumption of the cache quota and help build for multiple platforms from the same cache. Things to keep in mind while using this feature:

- Only cache files that are compatible across OSs.
- Caching symlinks might cause issues while restoring them as they behave differently on different OSs.
- Be mindful when caching files from outside your github workspace directory as the directory is located at different places across OS.
- Avoid using directory pointers such as `${{ github.workspace }}` or `~` (home) which eventually evaluate to an absolute path that does not match across OSs.

## Force deletion of caches overriding default cache eviction policy

Caches have [branch scope restriction](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/caching-dependencies-to-speed-up-workflows#restrictions-for-accessing-a-cache) in place. This means that if caches for a specific branch are using a lot of storage quota, it may result into more frequently used caches from `default` branch getting thrashed. For example, if there are many pull requests happening on a repo and are creating caches, these cannot be used in default branch scope but will still occupy a lot of space till they get cleaned up by [eviction policy](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/caching-dependencies-to-speed-up-workflows#usage-limits-and-eviction-policy). But sometime we want to clean them up on a faster cadence so as to ensure default branch is not thrashing.

<details>
  <summary>Example</summary>

```yaml
name: cleanup caches by a branch
on:
  pull_request:
    types:
      - closed
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  cleanup:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      # `actions:write` permission is required to delete caches
      #   See also: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/cache?apiVersion=2022-11-28#delete-a-github-actions-cache-for-a-repository-using-a-cache-id
      actions: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - name: Cleanup
        run: |
          echo "Fetching list of cache key"
          cacheKeysForPR=$(gh cache list --ref $BRANCH --limit 100 --json id --jq '.[].id')

          ## Setting this to not fail the workflow while deleting cache keys.
          set +e
          echo "Deleting caches..."
          for cacheKey in $cacheKeysForPR
          do
              gh cache delete $cacheKey
          done
          echo "Done"
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          BRANCH: refs/pull/${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}/merge
```

</details>

1	// Code-work, executor-side (docs/PRINCIPLES.md). The contract is
     2	// unchanged from the slot mechanism — a subprocess with the task dir as cwd, the
     3	// declared `code_work_required_secrets` as environment, a hard timeout, and the conditional
     4	// `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT` hand-off — so this module is a thin adapter that
     5	// gives the queue's item identity where the slot id used to go, and adds the two
     6	// things the queue states explicitly:
     7	//
     8	//  - RE-ENTRANCY IS THE REQUIREMENT, NOT IDEMPOTENCY (PRINCIPLES.md). A dead executor's
     9	//    claim is reclaimed and the item re-picked, so code-work can run again over its
    10	//    own half-done work. That is convergence — check what exists, continue from
    11	//    there — and it was always true of code-work; the contract simply never said so.
    12	//    Since the heartbeat replaced the run cap (PRINCIPLES.md), overlap is no longer
    13	//    excluded by construction: a partitioned runner keeps working while its beats
    14	//    fail to post, its claim is reclaimed on that silence, and the replacement
    15	//    starts. Re-entrancy is what makes that safe, which is why it is the contract.
    16	//  - A DECLARED SECRET THAT IS NOT CONFIGURED IS NAMED, NOT GUESSED AT (PRINCIPLES.md).
    17	//    Code-work is the only task code that ever sees a secret VALUE, so this is the
    18	//    one place that can tell "unset" from "empty", and the item converges to
    19	//    triage naming exactly which one is missing.
    20	
    21	import { runCodeWork, codeWorkFailure, agentRequestPath, clearAgentRequest, agentRequested, readAgentRequest, readTriageMarker, readRequeueMarker } from '../code-work.mjs';
    22	import { SECRETS_BAG_ENV, secretsBag, secretValue, secretsFor } from './secrets-bag.mjs';
    23	import { VARS_BAG_ENV, varsEnv } from './vars-bag.mjs';
    24	import { targetEnv } from './target.mjs';
    25	
    26	// The declared secrets this environment does not carry. Absent is missing; a
    27	// set-but-empty one is the repo's own choice and is passed through. Read through
    28	// the bag, which also answers for a legacy workflow that still stamps by name.
    29	export const missingSecrets = (names = [], env = process.env) =>
    30	  names.filter((n) => secretValue(n, env) === undefined);
    31	
    32	// The environment a task's work step runs under: this job's, minus every secret, plus
    33	// the ones this task declared, plus every repository variable.
    34	//
    35	// The two bags are treated differently on purpose. Secrets are SELECTED — the bag
    36	// carries the whole repository's, and a task's blast radius should be the list it wrote
    37	// down (#1336). Variables are not: `vars` is non-sensitive by construction, so there is
    38	// no blast radius to narrow and a declaration would buy nothing but a second place to
    39	// keep in sync. vars-bag.mjs states why they are additive rather than overriding.
    40	//
    41	// Under a workflow that names its secrets there is no bag to subtract, so the stamped
    42	// names stay inherited until that member's own executor workflow lands; the fallback in
    43	// secrets-bag.mjs states the retirement condition. Neither raw blob is ever handed on.
    44	export function taskEnv(names = [], env = process.env) {
    45	  const out = { ...env };
    46	  delete out[SECRETS_BAG_ENV];
    47	  delete out[VARS_BAG_ENV];
    48	  for (const name of Object.keys(secretsBag(env) ?? {})) delete out[name];
    49	  return { ...out, ...varsEnv(env), ...secretsFor(names, env) };
    50	}
    51	
    52	// The CLAUDINITE_* variables code-work is handed, and the whole of them: a worker
    53	// reading any other one is reading something nobody sets, which is silent and
    54	// permanent (a `CLAUDINITE_OVERRIDES` left over from the slot scheduler read as an
    55	// empty bag, so a fleet sweep's REPOS filter and DRY_RUN switch were inert and
    56	// every run was unscoped and live — #974).

Restrictions for accessing a cache

Access restrictions provide cache isolation and security by creating a logical boundary between different branches or tags. Workflow runs can restore caches created in either the current branch or the default branch (usually main). If a workflow run is triggered for a pull request, it can also restore caches created in the base branch, including base branches of forked repositories. For example, if the branch feature-b has the base branch feature-a, a workflow run triggered on a pull request would have access to caches created in the default main branch, the base feature-a branch, and the current feature-b branch.

Workflow runs cannot restore caches created for child branches or sibling branches. For example, a cache created for the child feature-b branch would not be accessible to a workflow run triggered on the parent main branch. Similarly, a cache created for the feature-a branch with the base main would not be accessible to its sibling feature-c branch with the base main. Workflow runs also cannot restore caches created for different tag names. For example, a cache created for the tag release-a with the base main would not be accessible to a workflow run triggered for the tag release-b with the base main.

When a cache is created by a workflow run triggered on a pull request, the cache is created for the merge ref (refs/pull/.../merge). Because of this, the cache will have a limited scope and can only be restored by re-runs of the pull request. It cannot be restored by the base branch or other pull requests targeting that base branch.

Multiple workflow runs in a repository can share caches. A cache created for a branch in a workflow run can be accessed and restored from another workflow run for the same repository and branch.

Cache access for low-trust workflow triggers

Some workflows run in response to events that can be initiated by people who do not have write access to the repository, such as a fork pull request or an issue comment. When these events run in the context of the default branch, they could be used to write a malicious cache that a later, more privileged workflow restores and trusts. This class of attack is known as cache poisoning.

To reduce this risk, only these workflow triggers can create or overwrite caches in the default branch’s scope:

  • push
  • workflow_dispatch
  • repository_dispatch
  • delete
  • registry_package
  • page_build
  • schedule

Runs triggered by any other event that resolves to the default branch are given read-only access to caches in the default branch's scope. These runs can restore existing caches but cannot create or overwrite them. This includes triggers whose payload or initiating actor can be influenced by someone outside the repository, such as pull_request_target, issue_comment, and workflow_run. A repository can opt out of this restriction for a specific workflow or job by explicitly declaring a write-capable cache-mode. See

---
name: ci-performance-evaluation
description: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
---

# Evaluating CI performance

The order below is the method, and the order is the point: each step tells you whether the next one
is worth doing. Most of what makes a suite slow is invisible from the top and obvious two steps
down, and most of what looks slow at the top is not where the time is.

## 1. Take the step breakdown before forming any theory

A job's own step timings are recorded — never guess from the total. List the run's jobs and read
each step's `started_at`/`completed_at`; the difference per step is the breakdown. Do this for
**several recent runs**, not one, so you know the spread before you call anything a regression.

State the split before going further ("checkout 4s, setup 5s, tests 48s, sweep 2s"). Only the
dominant step is worth profiling; time spent on a 2s step is time wasted whatever you find.

## 2. Reproduce the dominant step locally — and check the local run is comparable

Profile locally, but establish the gap first: a local run and a runner differ in core count, in
warm caches, and — the one that has actually bitten here — in **git commit signing**. A session
with signing configured pays a round trip per fixture commit that a runner never pays, so a local
profile can be dominated by a cost CI does not have. Compare a local total against the CI step
before trusting local numbers, and when they disagree, find out why *before* optimizing.

## 3. Find the long pole: time each test file serially

Time each file on its own, sum the results, and sort. That gives two numbers that matter: the
**serial total** (the work) and the **slowest single file** (the floor no amount of parallelism
gets under). Compare the serial total against the wall clock to see how much parallelism you are
already getting.

## 4. Read the distribution of per-test durations, not just the top of the list

Get every test's duration and bucket them. The shape tells you which kind of problem you have:

- **A few tests far above the rest** — specific slow cases. Read them; a test that waits seconds is
  usually waiting on something (see step 5).
- **A broad band of similar durations** — a *fixed per-test cost*, almost always in a shared fixture
  helper, and by far the more valuable find because it multiplies by every test in the band.
  Measure the helper directly rather than any one test.

## 5. Hunt the out-of-process waits

Time a suite spends waiting is not time it spends working, and it is the cheapest to remove. Look
for: subprocess spawns per test; sleeps and retry backoffs with hardcoded durations; calls to a
signing service, a network, a real git remote; anything with a timeout.

**A test that waits is often reporting a bug, not just being slow.** A test that sets a 0.3s
timeout and takes 10s is telling you the timeout does not work — the mechanism under test is
failing to kill what it claims to kill, and the 10s is the real lifetime leaking through. Chase
that reading before optimizing the test away: the same discipline found a `code_work_timeout` that
had never killed anything. Make a retry backoff injectable so tests scale the real timings down
rather than skip the path.

## 6. Check the parallelism headroom before adding parallelism

Compare wall clock against user+sys CPU time. Well under the core count means the suite is
*waiting*, so more workers help and oversubscribing beyond core count is right. At or near the core
count it is CPU-bound, and more workers buy nothing — including intra-file concurrency on the
longest file, which is the tempting move precisely when it is useless.

## 7. A/B every change against the whole suite, and revert what does not show

A change that halves one file routinely shows **zero** at suite level, because the cores were
already busy with other files. The file-level number is not the result; the suite-level number is.
Run both arms at least twice — a single pair inside normal variance is not a measurement. Complexity
that buys nothing measurable does not ship, and saying so is a finding, not a failure.

## 8. Verify in real CI, and report the two numbers separately

Local and CI improvements are different claims. Land the change, watch a real run, and give both
— "local 106s → 71s, CI 53s → 48s" — rather than letting the flattering one stand for both. When
they differ, explain the mechanism; a gap you cannot explain means the profile was measuring
something CI does not do.

## Reporting

Say where the time goes as a breakdown that adds up, name what you changed and what it bought,
and name what you deliberately left alone and why. A finding that an area is already fast is a
result worth stating — it stops the next person re-profiling it.

26:Removing a toolchain invites tidying away its ignore rules alongside it — but the artifacts it already produced are usually still sitting untracked in the worktree (`__pycache__/` from an earlier run, `build/` from an earlier build). The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps the junk *into* the commit that was supposed to remove it, and nothing complains: the commit is valid and the tests still pass. Delete (or `git clean`) the artifacts first, then drop their ignore lines. And after any bulk `git add -A`, read `git diff --cached --stat` — staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops telling you about.
116:GitHub suppresses workflow runs triggered by the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to prevent recursion, so a workflow's own `git push` or `gh pr create` won't fire another workflow (e.g. a `test` or cache-refresh workflow). The one exception is `workflow_dispatch` / `repository_dispatch` — which is why an automation pipeline that needs the downstream checks to run must dispatch them explicitly. A run dispatched against a branch executes on its head commit, so its checks still attach to the PR. The same suppression covers a Claude session's own app-scoped pushes: creating a PR through the API does fire its `pull_request` run, but a follow-up push to that PR gets **no** `synchronize` run — so don't wait for checks that will never start on the new head; gate by running the CI commands locally, and rely on the post-merge run (merging through the merge API does fire the `push` workflow on the default branch).

busy-wait-loop — an action guard over Bash. The #1932 session waited on a

never arrived, the empty body never yielded, and the loop held the session for

and was silent here.

push nothing when it matches; a force-push discards the checks already run.

entries.name: mcp__github__actions_get
entries.description:
Get details about specific GitHub Actions resources.
Use this tool to get details about individual workflows, workflow runs, jobs, and artifacts by their unique IDs.

resource_id.description:
The unique identifier of the resource. This will vary based on the "method" provided, so ensure you provide the correct ID:
- Provide a workflow ID or workflow file name (e.g. ci.yaml) for 'get_workflow' method.
- Provide a workflow run ID for 'get_workflow_run', 'get_workflow_run_usage', and 'get_workflow_run_logs_url' methods.
- Provide an artifact ID for 'download_workflow_run_artifact' method.
- Provide a job ID for 'get_workflow_job' method.

entries.name: mcp__github__actions_list
entries.description:
Tools for listing GitHub Actions resources.
Use this tool to list workflows in a repository, or list workflow runs, jobs, and artifacts for a specific workflow or workflow run.

# Find out why CI got slower, and fix it if it is worth fixing

You are here because code-work measured this repo's CI and found at least one workflow whose median
duration this week is materially above the week before. The dispatch names the workflow and the
before/after; the standing tracker — the issue the work item's **Delivered by code-work** section names
(`Issue: #<n>`) — carries the full table and the step breakdown of the slowest run, written there by
code-work before you started.

**That number is a required input.** A work item that does not carry it is a failed run, not a lighter one: park it (`task:status:needs-human-action`) naming the missing input.
Do not search for the tracker by title and do not open one — code-work already wrote this run's
measurements to a specific issue, and any issue you find yourself is a different one.

The whole of *how* is the [ci-performance-evaluation](../../skills/ci-performance-evaluation/SKILL.md)
skill. Follow it in order — it is written so each step tells you whether the next is worth doing.
Don't re-derive it here.

## What is yours in particular

- **The regression is a claim to test, not a fact to act on.** Code-work compared two medians; it did
  not establish a cause, and runner weather, a new test suite, or a genuinely bigger repo all move
  a median. Confirm the change is real and attributable before optimizing anything, and if it is
  not, say so on the tracker and stop — that is a complete outcome.
- **Find the cause before the fix.** The skill's steps 3–5 exist because the obvious suspect is
  usually wrong. A broad band of similar-duration tests means a shared fixture cost, not a slow
  test; a test that waits on a timeout is often reporting a bug in the thing it tests.
- **A/B against the whole suite and revert what does not show** (step 7). A change that helps one
  file and nothing overall does not ship.
- **Report both numbers separately** (step 8): what changed locally and what changed in a real CI
  run, with the mechanism for any gap.

## Landing it

One PR. CI itself is the gate: a run that turns anything red cannot merge, and a green one may land
unattended. Reference the tracker issue in the PR body, and comment the PR link on the tracker so
the week the regression was open is legible afterwards.

If the honest answer is that the regression is real and not worth fixing — the suite grew because
the repo grew — write that on the tracker with the numbers behind it and open no PR. A measurement
that concludes "this is the correct cost" is the point of taking the measurement.

## What you must not do

- **Deliver on the branch and pull request your item names — that is the deliverable.** Push to `Target-branch:`, and onto `Target-pr:` where one is named, so this round joins the review already pending; open the PR on that branch where none is named. Never search for an open pull request or pick a branch of your own. What happens to it after that is the delivery machinery's, not this run's.
- **Never make a test weaker to make it faster** — deleting coverage, dropping a case, loosening an
  assertion, or excluding a suite from the run. If a test genuinely costs more than it is worth,
  that is an argument to put to the owner on the tracker, not a change to land here.
########## README
# ci-performance

## Why the declaration reads as it does

Carried over from the declaration's comments when it became `task.json`.

basics task: ci-performance — the weekly read on where this repo's CI time goes,
and whether it has got worse.

A suite's runtime degrades the way a lawn grows: never in one visible step, so
nobody profiles it until it is bad enough to complain about, by which point the
cause is a dozen changes back. This task takes the measurement on a cadence
instead, from the one ledger that cannot be argued with — the Actions run
history — and keeps a standing record of it.

CONDITIONAL HANDOFF. Code-work does the measuring, which is pure code: read the
runs, take each workflow's median over this window and the one before, compare.
A quiet week ends there — the record is refreshed and no agent is spent. Only a
real regression requests the agent, which then has something worth its time: a
named workflow, a before and after, and the ci-performance-evaluation skill's
method for finding the cause.

WHY sonnet: the finding arrives already localized to a workflow and a delta, and
the skill states the method step by step; what remains is profiling and a bounded
fix. Ceilinged at `pr`; what it may land unattended is the `automerge` policy below.

Movement, not standing state: CI runtime only changes when something lands, so
a week where nothing moved has the same runs, the same medians and the same
verdict as last week.
A couple of hundred run records plus one job breakdown, against this repo's own
API. Seconds in practice; the bound is for a rate-limited or wedged read.
Profiling a suite means running it, more than once, in both arms of an A/B.

content.content:
# Headless browser

## Getting a browser

- **Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container
  or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry
  download is slow, often blocked, and pins a build you did not choose. Look for an explicit
  override variable first, then the image's browser root, then fall through to the driver's own
  resolution — and prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all. The
  image's build number need not match the driver's own pin for the browser to launch. Never
  hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the
  failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it.

- **A fresh install of the driver package is the same danger from upstream.** Reinstalling the
  package to fix an import error just as easily resolves to a newer release than the one paired
  with the environment's pinned browser — it then hunts for a browser build the image was never
  given and fails asking for a network install the sandbox cannot make. A reinstall run from the
  repo root instead of a scratchpad can dodge that failure outright (a version happens to
  resolve that works) and still cost you: it dirties the tracked `package.json`, its lockfile and
  `node_modules`, which then need a manual revert before anything can be committed. Resolve the
=== aws-sam 28,45 ===
  non-simple header (e.g. a client-version header) makes the browser send an `OPTIONS` preflight, so
  the API's CORS `AllowHeaders` must list that header or the real request is blocked *in the
  browser* — while server-side unit tests that never run the CORS layer stay green.

- **Reach AWS from a session with the AWS CLI or a boto3 script — there is no AWS MCP tool.** A
  stack's real state comes from a CLI call (`aws cloudformation describe-stacks …`) — the last
  green deploy workflow only reports the last *deploy*, not the current stack state. The CLI is
  **not pre-installed on the cloud/web runner** (nor `boto3`/`sam`), so declare its install in the
  **environment setup script** (`pip install awscli`, or the official bundle) rather than per
  session; point it at the sandbox proxy's CA bundle (`AWS_CA_BUNDLE`) if a call fails TLS
  verification.
=== flutter 50,62 ===
  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.

- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.

- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.

method.description:
The read operation to perform on a single issue.
Options are:
1. get - Get issue details. 3. get_sub_issues - Get sub-issues (children) of the issue.
4. get_parent - Get the parent issue, if this issue is a sub-issue of another.
5. get_labels - Get labels assigned to the issue.

## 1. Workflow YAML the canon ships or runs

### Canon's own — `/home/user/Claudinite/.github/workflows/`

| File | Setup/install steps | Caching |
|---|---|---|
| `ci.yml` | `actions/checkout@v4` with **`fetch-depth: 0`** (`ci.yml:20-28`); `actions/setup-node@v4`, `node-version: 20` (`ci.yml:29-31`). No npm/pip step at all. | **None.** No `cache:` key, no `actions/cache`. |
| `canary-rehearsal.yml` | `actions/checkout@v5` ×2 (canon + canary repo, `:73-102`); `actions/setup-node@v5`, `node-version: '24'` (`:104-107`). The rehearse step then shells a **second, independent `git clone --depth 1` of the canon** inside `update/worker.mjs`. | **None.** |
| `claudinite-executor.yml` | `actions/checkout@v5` + `actions/setup-node@v5` `node-version: 24` in both jobs (`:37-40`, `:75-78`). No install. | **None.** |
| `claudinite-scheduler.yml` | Same checkout + setup-node 24 in all three jobs (`:34-36`, `:56-58`, `:78-80`). | **None.** |
| `pack-versions.yml` | `actions/checkout@v5` with **`fetch-depth: 0`** (`:28-32` — comment: "The worker walks main back to each pack's last bump; a one-commit checkout would unshallow itself"); setup-node 24 (`:33-35`). | **None.** |

Relevant fact: the canon has **no `package.json` anywhere in the tree** (verified) — so `setup-node`'s `cache: npm` would have nothing to key on. The cacheable costs here are the two `fetch-depth: 0` full-history checkouts and the canon clone in the rehearsal.

### Generated by `packs/claudinite-tasks/converge-workflows.mjs`

It generates exactly two files, from stubs, never from scratch:
- `SCHEDULER_WORKFLOW = '.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml'` (`converge-workflows.mjs:24`)
- `EXECUTOR_WORKFLOW = '.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml'` (`converge-workflows.mjs:28`)

Sources: `packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-scheduler.yml` and `.../claudinite-executor.yml`. The converge only (a) stamps secret env lines at the `# claudinite:secrets` marker (`:80-98`) and (b) rewrites the cron (`:104-107`). It **never touches the setup steps**, so any caching added to the stubs propagates to the whole fleet on the next scaffold — but note `converge-workflows.mjs:6-12`: "**SCAFFOLDED, NEVER CONVERGED** … these two files arrive once, at adoption … and the repo owns them from that moment." A cache change in the stubs would therefore *not* reach already-adopted members.

Stub contents (setup/caching):
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-scheduler.yml:33-36, 55-58, 77-80` — `actions/checkout@v5` + `actions/setup-node@v5` `node-version: 24`, three times. No cache.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/stubs/claudinite-executor.yml:37-40, 70-73` — same, twice. No cache. `timeout-minutes: 350` (`:35`).

### Pack stub workflows (`packs/*/stubs/workflows/*.yml`)

Only four packs ship workflow stubs: `chrome-extension`, `static-website`, `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-canary-repo`.

**chrome-extension**
- `chrome-extension-create-package.yml:73-77` — the **only caching anywhere in the repo**:
  ```yaml
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
    with:
      node-version: 22
      # npm caching needs a lockfile; a repo that skips install has none.
      cache: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.setup_command != '' && 'npm' || '' }}
  ```
  Install at `:79-81` (`run: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.setup_command }}`), test gate at `:136-138`, `npm run build` twice at `:161` and `:164`.
- `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml:69-71` — `setup-node@v5` `node-version: 22`, **no `cache:`**; `:122` `npx --yes chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3 upload` (uncached npx download every publish).
- `chrome-extension-bump-version.yml:47-63` — checkout + two local composite actions, no node setup, no install.
- `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml:38` — "The check job runs on a bare runner (no npm ci)".
- `deploy-privacy-page.yml` — no node, no install.

**static-website**
- `static-site-ci.yml:35-43` — checkout `fetch-depth: 0` + `setup-node@v5` `node-version: 22`, **no `cache:`**, no install step; the repo's `test_command` (`:51-53`) and `build_command` (`:65-67`) are free-form and are expected to run their own `npm ci`.
- `static-site-deploy-pages.yml:58-61` — conditional `setup-node@v5` 22, no cache; `:73-77`:
  ```
  # A build_command that needs dependencies installs them itself
  # (`npm ci && npm run build`) — see the config's keys.
  ```
- `static-site-publish.yml:116-121` — explicit refusal:
  ```
  # No install step and no npm cache: a test_command that needs dependencies
  # says so itself (`npm ci && npm test`), which keeps the config to the five
  # keys and never assumes a lockfile a plain HTML repo doesn't have.
  ```
- `static-site-bump-version.yml`, `static-site-release.yml` — orchestration only, no setup.

**claudinite-dashboard** — `stubs/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml:31-39`: checkout, `configure-pages@v5`, `upload-pages-artifact@v3`, `deploy-pages@v4`. No node, no install, no cache.

**claudinite-canary-repo** — `stubs/workflows/claudinite-workflow-probe.yml:36`: a single `echo`. Nothing to cache.

No `actions/cache` appears anywhere in the repository (grepped `--include=*.yml --include=*.md`: zero hits).

## 2. How the agentic phase gets a Claude Code CLI — it doesn't

**Nothing installs a package for the agent.** Grepping `packs/claudinite-tasks` for `claude-code|@anthropic-ai|npm install|npm ci|npx ` across `.mjs`/`.md`/`.json` (excluding tests) returns **zero hits**. There is no CLI in the Actions job.

The agentic phase is a single outbound HTTP call to Claude Code Remote:
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/invoke.mjs:26-28` — "The endpoint is a ROUTINE'S API TRIGGER — `POST /v1/claude_code/routines/<trigger-id>/fire` with a per-routine bearer token — which is what Claude Code on the web actually exposes to an HTTP caller."
- `invoke.mjs:56-59` — `DEFAULT_HEADERS` = `anthropic-beta: experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01`, `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`.
- `invoke.mjs:43-46` — "THIS MODULE CALLS ONCE PER ITEM AND NEVER RETRIES."
- `invoke.mjs:64-79` — `resolveEndpoint()`: URL and token-secret name come from `taskScheduler.<endpoints>` in the repo's settings.

The executor **hands off and exits** — it does not wait for the session (`queue/executor.mjs:532`, `:541` → `handOff(...)`; `:593-595` "Hand off to an agent session … ONE call per item, ever"). So no polling of the agent from the job.

Where the executor job's wall clock actually goes:
1. `actions/checkout@v5` + `actions/setup-node@v5` (fixed, ~seconds).
2. **GitHub REST calls** — `listOpenWorkItems`, `listComments`, label swaps, PATCHes: `executor.mjs:237, 244-247, 265-269, 509, 611`; `github.mjs:20-113` (`per_page=100` comment paging at `github.mjs:71`).
3. **The task's `code_work` subprocess** — `code-work.mjs:59` `spawn(command, { cwd: taskDir, env, shell: true, detached: true })`, bounded by `code_work_timeout` (`code-work.mjs:66`). Every declared task is `"code_work": "node worker.mjs"` (17 task.json files). This is where the real time is.
4. **A 15-minute heartbeat comment loop** while code-work runs — `queue/heartbeat.mjs:26` `HEARTBEAT_MS = 15 * 60e3`, driven at `executor.mjs:453-454`. Not a poll of anything; a keepalive write.

Git/network heavy things inside code-work (all in the Actions job, all uncached):
- `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs:189-190` — `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite.git` (`CANON_URL` at `:28`) into a fresh tmpdir, **every update cycle, in every member**. This is the single biggest recurring fetch in the fleet.
- `packs/claudinite-canon-curation/tasks/pack-version-bump/worker.mjs:33-40` — `fetchBase()` does `git fetch --unshallow` when shallow: "Unshallowing is a fetch the size of the repository once and a no-op after."
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/worker.mjs:141-158` — `deepenHistory()`, `git fetch --shallow-since=<window>`.
- `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-add-missing-packs/canon-packs.mjs:61-63` — another `git clone --depth 1 --quiet` of the canon into a scratch dir.
- `packs/cloudflare-site/tasks/site-release/worker.mjs:31` `export const WRANGLER = 'wrangler@4.128.0';` and `:177` `execFileSync('npx', ['--yes', WRANGLER, 'deploy'], …)` — **the one package download in an Actions job**, pinned and re-fetched every release.

## 3. What the CI/perf prose already says about caching

`packs/basics/skills/ci-performance-evaluation/SKILL.md` — **caching is never proposed as a fix.** The word appears once, only as a confounder when comparing local vs CI (`SKILL.md:23-24`): "a local run and a runner differ in core count, in **warm caches**, and — the one that has actually bitten here — in **git commit signing**." The eight steps are: step breakdown (`:13`), reproduce locally (`:21`), time each test file serially (`:31`), read the duration distribution (`:37`), hunt out-of-process waits (`:46`), check parallelism headroom (`:56`), A/B against the whole suite (`:63`), verify in real CI (`:70`). There is no setup/install/dependency-restore step in the method — it is entirely a test-suite-profiling method.

`packs/basics/tasks/ci-performance/task.md` / `README.md` / `worker.mjs` / `task.json` — **zero mentions of caching** (grepped). `task.md:13-14` delegates wholly to the skill: "The whole of *how* is the ci-performance-evaluation skill. Follow it in order … Don't re-derive it here." `README.md` describes code-work as reading run medians from the Actions API and only handing to an agent on a real regression.

`packs/git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md` — no caching guidance. The only hit is incidental at `:116`: "a workflow's own `git push` or `gh pr create` won't fire another workflow (e.g. a `test` or **cache-refresh** workflow)". `:26` mentions `__pycache__/` in an ignore-rules context.

## 4. `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs` and vendoring

**Mechanism: a fresh shallow `git clone` over HTTPS, no token, no tarball, no API.**

- `worker.mjs:28` — `const CANON_URL = 'https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite.git'; // public — no token`
- `worker.mjs:183-190`:
  ```
  // The flows run from a FRESH CANON CLONE, never from this repo's mount: the mount is
  // the thing being replaced, and a flow executing its own stale copy is how a broken
  // update makes itself permanent.
  const tmp = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'claudinite-canon-'));
  …
  git(rehearsalRef
    ? ['clone', '--depth', '1', '--branch', rehearsalRef, CANON_URL, tmp]
    : ['clone', '--depth', '1', CANON_URL, tmp]);
  ```
- It then imports the flows **out of the clone** (`:191-194`): `engine-update.mjs`, `pack-update.mjs`, `terminals.mjs`.
- `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/engine-update.mjs:49` and `pack-update.mjs:43` derive `canonRoot` from `import.meta.url`, and the actual vendoring is plain `copyFileSync(join(canonRoot, file), dest)` (`engine-update.mjs:178`, `pack-update.mjs:230`) plus template reads (`:188`, `:269`). So **the whole mount is served from that one clone's working tree** — no further network.
- The member's own branch fetch is separately shallow: `worker.mjs:266` `git(['-C', root, 'fetch', '--depth', '1', remote, 'refs/heads/'+branch])`.
- Rehearsal mode restores the tree afterwards (`worker.mjs:218-220`).

Cacheability: the clone is `--depth 1` of the default branch, so its content is a pure function of the canon's head SHA — a per-canon-ref cache key (restore the tmp tree keyed on the resolved canon SHA) is exactly the shape `actions/cache` wants. Note the double cost in `canary-rehearsal.yml`: the workflow already checks out the canon at `:73` *and* the worker clones it again at `worker.mjs:189`. Note also `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs:90, 106` describe the flows as applying "from the fresh canon clone … where every record ever landed is" — worth confirming a depth-1 clone actually carries what those records need.

## 5. Tech packs: CI advice and caching

None of `node`, `python`, `flutter`, `android`, `ios`, `headless-browser`, `cloudflare-workers`, `aws-sam` ships a `stubs/` directory at all. `static-website` and `cloudflare-site` are the only two here with CI-adjacent shipped artifacts (`static-website/stubs/workflows/*`, covered in §1; `cloudflare-site/tasks/site-release/`).

| Pack | Ships CI/stubs? | Caching mentioned? |
|---|---|---|
| `node` | No stubs. One CI rule: `RULES.md:28-31` — "check what version CI actually pins — the workflow's `setup-node` step, not the Node installed in the sandbox". | **No.** |
| `python` | No stubs. `RULES.md` has **no** `pip`/`venv`/`requirements`/CI hits at all. | **No.** |
| `flutter` | No stubs. `RULES.md:56-59` — "**Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers"; the fix is a kill-on-marker wrapper, not caching. No `pub get`/`.pub-cache` *CI* advice. | Only the pub cache as a **read path** for API verification: `RULES.md:49-50` "resolved versions live in the pub cache (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`)", echoed in `README.md:7`. Not a CI caching rule. |
| `android` | README + `pack.mjs` only — **no RULES.md**, no gradle advice, no caching. | **No.** |
| `ios` | No stubs. `RULES.md:5` — "a change counts as verified only once the macOS CI runner … " (Swift builds). No xcode/DerivedData caching. | **No.** |
| `headless-browser` | No stubs. `RULES.md:4-12` is directly caching-adjacent but argues the *opposite* direction: "**Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry download is slow, often blocked … prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all." `:13-22` warns a driver reinstall re-resolves to a browser the image lacks. | No `actions/cache`; the stated remedy is image-provided browsers, not a cached download. |
| `static-website` | Five workflow stubs + three composite-action stubs. | Only the two explicit *refusals* quoted in §1 (`static-site-publish.yml:116-118`, `static-site-deploy-pages.yml:73-74`). `RULES.md:30-54` is entirely about **HTTP `Cache-Control`/CDN** freshness, not CI. |
| `cloudflare-site` | No workflow stubs; ships the `site-release` task that runs `npx --yes wrangler@4.128.0 deploy` in the executor job (`tasks/site-release/worker.mjs:31, 177`). | **No.** |
| `cloudflare-workers` | README/RULES only, no stubs. `RULES.md` CI hits are about Cloudflare *Workflows* (the product), not Actions. | **No.** |
| `aws-sam` | No stubs. `RULES.md:32-38` — "The CLI is **not pre-installed on the cloud/web runner** (nor `boto3`/`sam`), so declare its install in the **environment setup script** (`pip install awscli`, or the official bundle) rather than per session". That is Claude-Code-sandbox setup guidance, not Actions. | `references.md:21-23` and `skills/sam-template/SKILL.md:12-27` are **CloudFront cache-policy** guidance, unrelated to CI. |

### Summary of the caching surface as it stands

One `cache:` key exists in the entire corpus — `packs/chrome-extension/stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-create-package.yml:77` — and it is conditional on a lockfile existing. Everything else is uncached by decision (static-website's two comments) or by omission (all five canon workflows, both claudinite-tasks stubs, chrome-extension's publish job). The largest uncached repeat costs are: the canon `git clone --depth 1` per update cycle per member (`update/worker.mjs:189-190`), the two `fetch-depth: 0` checkouts in canon CI (`ci.yml:20-22`, `pack-versions.yml:28-32`), the `--unshallow` in `pack-version-bump/worker.mjs:38`, and the two pinned `npx --yes` downloads (`cloudflare-site/tasks/site-release/worker.mjs:177`, `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml:122`). No prose anywhere in the corpus tells anyone to cache any of it.

input.title: GitHub Actions cache: where it helps Claudinite's machinery and members, and where it doesn't
input.body:
Analysis of the GitHub Actions cache offering against this repo's real run ledger and the pack corpus. No code changed; this issue records the findings and the candidate actions for the owner to pick from.

## The offering, as GitHub documents it today

- `actions/cache` (v6; also `cache/restore` and `cache/save` for split control), and `setup-node` / `setup-python` / `setup-java` / `setup-go` `cache:` inputs that key on a lockfile.
- 10 GB per repository free; entries not accessed for **7 days** are evicted.
- A cache is **branch-scoped**: a run reads its own branch, then the default branch. A cache written by a `pull_request` run lands under `refs/pull/N/merge` and is reusable only by re-runs of that PR. To be useful across branches, a `push` (or `schedule` / `workflow_dispatch`) run on the default branch must write it.
- **Low-trust triggers** (`issues`, `issue_comment`, `workflow_run`, `pull_request_target`, …) get **read-only** access to the default-branch scope unless the job declares `cache-mode: write`. This directly concerns the executor workflow, which is triggered by `issues: labeled`.
- A cache is immutable per key; "updating" means a unique key plus `restore-keys` prefix fallback, which burns quota per run.

## What the canon's own jobs actually spend (run ledger, 2026-09-13)

| Workflow | Total | Setup (checkout + setup-node) | Real work |
|---|---|---|---|
| CI | ~150 s | 11 s (`fetch-depth: 0` checkout 7 s, setup-node 4 s) | unit tests 131 s, sweeps 3 s |
| Scheduler (`scheduler-run`) | ~5 min | 3 s | precondition signal collection ~4 m 40 s, all GitHub API reads |
| Executor (`execute`) | ~20 s | 2 s | queue reads and the Claude Code Remote dispatch, ~15 s |

- The canon has no `package.json`; nothing installs. The runner image already has Node. **A dependency cache has nothing to hold here.**
- Every declared task's `code_work` is `node worker.mjs`; the agentic phase is one HTTP call to Claude Code Remote and the job exits. **The executor job is not where agent time goes**, so a runner cache cannot help the tasks executor's main cost.

## Where the minutes really go: the scheduler's API round-trips

`packs/claudinite-tasks/signals/index.mjs` `windowCommits` does one `/repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}` read per commit in the window, and `collectSignals` is called **per task**, so the same commit is re-read once per task (13 tasks this run; the weekly tasks each saw 40 commits). Hundreds of sequential API calls ≈ 4.5 minutes, and members pay the same shape nightly.

Three fixes, in order of value; only the third is an Actions cache:
1. **In-run memo** of commit-detail reads keyed by sha, shared across tasks. One read per commit per run. Small code change in the signals collector; no cache infra.
2. **Read from git instead of the API**: a `fetch-depth: 0` checkout costs 7 s in CI and `git log --name-only --since` answers the whole window with zero API calls. Changes the scheduler stub's checkout depth, which is workflow content (lands only via a migration record).
3. **Persist the memo across runs** with `actions/cache/restore` + `save` around the run step, keyed on the default-branch sha with a prefix `restore-keys`. The scheduler runs on `schedule` / `workflow_dispatch`, so it may write default-branch caches; the executor (an `issues`-triggered, read-only run) could read the same warmed cache. This is the one shape in which the executor benefits from a cache at all. Cost: 7-day eviction means a weekly-only warmer would lose it; the twice-daily scheduler keeps it warm.

## Other repeated fetches, judged

- `claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs` clones the canon `--depth 1` per member per cycle. The canon's packed objects are a few MB; the clone is seconds. Restoring a cache tarball costs about the same. **Not worth caching.** (The canary workflow does clone the canon twice, once in checkout and once in the worker; a wasted few seconds, not a cache problem.)
- `pack-version-bump` unshallows and `pack-versions.yml` uses `fetch-depth: 0`: 7 s each. Not worth caching.
- `cloudflare-site/tasks/site-release/worker.mjs` runs `npx --yes wrangler@4.128.0` and `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` runs `npx --yes chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3`: a pinned download per release, tens of seconds. Cacheable via `actions/cache` on `~/.npm` keyed on the pinned version, but the executor job is read-only on default scope, so it needs `cache-mode: write` or a warmer. Low value; record as an option.

## Where the value is: advice to members

The corpus has exactly one `cache:` line (`packs/chrome-extension/stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-create-package.yml`, conditional on a lockfile). The `node`, `python`, `flutter`, `android`, `ios` packs say nothing about CI caching. `static-website` stubs refuse it explicitly so as not to assume a lockfile. The `ci-performance-evaluation` skill profiles tests only; it has no step that asks whether setup and install dominate the run.

Candidate advice, each to be verified against a real run before it is written (basics rule: never document a path not run):
- `node`: `setup-node` with `cache: ${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') != '' && 'npm' || '' }}`, the conditional form chrome-extension already uses; also that setup-node now auto-enables npm caching when `package.json` declares `packageManager`, so a repo without a lockfile must set `package-manager-cache: false` or the step fails. `static-website`'s two stubs could take the same conditional form without adding a config key.
- `python`: `setup-python` `cache: pip` keyed on `requirements*.txt`.
- `android`: `gradle/actions/setup-gradle` caching. `flutter`: the pub cache via the Flutter setup action's cache input. `ios`: SPM / DerivedData caching is contentious; probably a note that it rarely pays.
- `headless-browser`: the existing rule (use the image's browser, never let the driver download) stands; a browser cache is the fallback only where the image lacks the browser.
- `ci-performance-evaluation` skill: a step 0 that reads the setup-versus-work split and sends install-dominated runs to caching rather than to test profiling.
- `git-github-advanced` skill: the three scoping gotchas above (PR-scope writes, low-trust read-only, 7-day eviction), since each silently makes a cache a no-op.

## Decisions for the owner

1. Fix the scheduler's per-task commit re-reads (memo, git-based read, or persisted cache)? Recommendation: the in-run memo first; it removes most of the cost with no workflow change.
2. Author the member-facing caching advice in the tech packs and the two skills?
3. Cache the pinned `npx` downloads in release tasks (needs `cache-mode: write` on the executor job)? Recommendation: no, until a release task's duration is a complaint.

**The short answer: the Actions cache buys almost nothing for Claudinite's own machinery, and its value here is in advice to members.** The canon's jobs carry no dependency install, and the agentic phase leaves Actions entirely.

**What the run ledger shows for this repo**

| Workflow | Total | Setup | Real work |
|---|---|---|---|
| CI | ~150 s | 11 s | tests 131 s |
| Scheduler | ~5 min | 3 s | precondition API reads ~4 m 40 s |
| Executor | ~20 s | 2 s | queue reads + one Claude Code Remote dispatch |

- **CI has nothing to cache.** No `package.json`, Node is on the image, and the 131 s is the test suite.
- **The executor is not where task time goes.** Every task's `code_work` is `node worker.mjs`, and the agent runs on Claude Code Remote after a single HTTP call.
- **The scheduler's minutes are API round-trips, not downloads.** The commit-window collector reads one commit-detail endpoint per commit and is invoked once per task, so 13 tasks re-read the same 40 commits. The best fix is an in-run memo keyed by sha, with no cache infrastructure. A `fetch-depth: 0` checkout plus `git log` would remove the API calls entirely. Persisting the memo through `actions/cache` is the third option and the only shape in which the executor benefits from a cache at all.

**Three offering facts that shape any use here**

- A cache written by a `pull_request` run lives under the PR's merge ref and is reusable only by that PR's re-runs. Only a `push`, `schedule` or `workflow_dispatch` run on the default branch writes a cache other branches can read.
- Low-trust triggers get read-only access to the default-branch scope unless the job declares `cache-mode: write`. The executor is `issues: labeled`, so it can read a cache the scheduler warms but cannot write one.
- Entries unused for 7 days are evicted, so a weekly-only warmer loses its cache every week.

**Other repeated fetches, judged not worth caching**: the update worker's depth-1 canon clone per member (seconds, and a cache restore costs the same), the two full-history checkouts (7 s each), and the pinned `npx` downloads in the cloudflare-site and chrome-extension release paths (tens of seconds, and they would need `cache-mode: write`).

**Where the value is**: the corpus has one `cache:` line in the whole tree, in the chrome-extension package stub. The node, python, flutter, android and ios packs say nothing about CI caching, the static-website stubs refuse it to avoid assuming a lockfile, and the ci-performance skill profiles tests without ever asking whether setup dominates. The issue lists the candidate advice per pack and the two skill additions, each to be verified against a real run before being written.

> ⚠️ Still open: the three decisions in [#2012](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2012). Fix the scheduler's per-task commit re-reads (recommended: the in-run memo first)? Author the member-facing caching advice in the tech packs and skills? Cache the pinned `npx` downloads (recommended: no)?

input.title: Scheduler re-reads each window commit's detail once per task
input.body:
`windowCommits` in `packs/claudinite-tasks/signals/index.mjs` reads `/repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}` for every commit in the window, and `collectSignals` runs once per task, so one scheduler run reads the same commit's detail once per task that windows on commits. Requirement: within one process, a commit's detail is read from the API at most once, however many tasks (or executor picks) collect commit-derived signals. A read that did not return 200 is not memoised, so a rate limit or a 5xx is retried by the next collector rather than pinned for the run.

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative. A bash glob without `globstar` is the dangerous
  substitute — it reached 37 of 65 files and reported nothing wrong — while `node --test <dir>`
  fails outright, so only the glob leaves you believing a green run. (4)
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (1)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which. (2)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (3)

{"id":5443277203,"number":2012,"state":"open","locked":false,"title":"GitHub Actions cache: where it helps Claudinite's machinery and members, and where it doesn't","body":"Analysis of the GitHub Actions cache offering against this repo's real run ledger and the pack corpus. No code changed; this issue records the findings and the candidate actions for the owner to pick from.

## The offering, as GitHub documents it today

- `actions/cache` (v6; also `cache/restore` and `cache/save` for split control), and `setup-node` / `setup-python` / `setup-java` / `setup-go` `cache:` inputs that key on a lockfile.
- 10 GB per repository free; entries not accessed for **7 days** are evicted.
- A cache is **branch-scoped**: a run reads its own branch, then the default branch. A cache written by a `pull_request` run lands under `refs/pull/N/merge` and is reusable only by re-runs of that PR. To be useful across branches, a `push` (or `schedule` / `workflow_dispatch`) run on the default branch must write it.
- **Low-trust triggers** (`issues`, `issue_comment`, `workflow_run`, `pull_request_target`, …) get **read-only** access to the default-branch scope unless the job declares `cache-mode: write`. This directly concerns the executor workflow, which is triggered by `issues: labeled`.
- A cache is immutable per key; "updating" means a unique key plus `restore-keys` prefix fallback, which burns quota per run.

## What the canon's own jobs actually spend (run ledger, 2026-09-13)

| Workflow | Total | Setup (checkout + setup-node) | Real work |
|---|---|---|---|
| CI | ~150 s | 11 s (`fetch-depth: 0` checkout 7 s, setup-node 4 s) | unit tests 131 s, sweeps 3 s |
| Scheduler (`scheduler-run`) | ~5 min | 3 s | precondition signal collection ~4 m 40 s, all GitHub API reads |
| Executor (`execute`) | ~20 s | 2 s | queue reads and the Claude Code Remote dispatch, ~15 s |

- The canon has no `package.json`; nothing installs. The runner image already has Node. **A dependency cache has nothing to hold here.**
- Every declared task's `code_work` is `node worker.mjs`; the agentic phase is one HTTP call to Claude Code Remote and the job exits. **The executor job is not where agent time goes**, so a runner cache cannot help the tasks executor's main cost.

## Where the minutes really go: the scheduler's API round-trips

`packs/claudinite-tasks/signals/index.mjs` `windowCommits` does one `/repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}` read per commit in the window, and `collectSignals` is called **per task**, so the same commit is re-read once per task (13 tasks this run; the weekly tasks each saw 40 commits). Hundreds of sequential API calls ≈ 4.5 minutes, and members pay the same shape nightly.

Three fixes, in order of value; only the third is an Actions cache:
1. **In-run memo** of commit-detail reads keyed by sha, shared across tasks. One read per commit per run. Small code change in the signals collector; no cache infra.
2. **Read from git instead of the API**: a `fetch-depth: 0` checkout costs 7 s in CI and `git log --name-only --since` answers the whole window with zero API calls. Changes the scheduler stub's checkout depth, which is workflow content (lands only via a migration record).
3. **Persist the memo across runs** with `actions/cache/restore` + `save` around the run step, keyed on the default-branch sha with a prefix `restore-keys`. The scheduler runs on `schedule` / `workflow_dispatch`, so it may write default-branch caches; the executor (an `issues`-triggered, read-only run) could read the same warmed cache. This is the one shape in which the executor benefits from a cache at all. Cost: 7-day eviction means a weekly-only warmer would lose it; the twice-daily scheduler keeps it warm.

## Other repeated fetches, judged

- `claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs` clones the canon `--depth 1` per member per cycle. The canon's packed objects are a few MB; the clone is seconds. Restoring a cache tarball costs about the same. **Not worth caching.** (The canary workflow does clone the canon twice, once in checkout and once in the worker; a wasted few seconds, not a cache problem.)
- `pack-version-bump` unshallows and `pack-versions.yml` uses `fetch-depth: 0`: 7 s each. Not worth caching.
- `cloudflare-site/tasks/site-release/worker.mjs` runs `npx --yes wrangler@4.128.0` and `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` runs `npx --yes chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3`: a pinned download per release, tens of seconds. Cacheable via `actions/cache` on `~/.npm` keyed on the pinned version, but the executor job is read-only on default scope, so it needs `cache-mode: write` or a warmer. Low value; record as an option.

## Where the value is: advice to members

The corpus has exactly one `cache:` line (`packs/chrome-extension/stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-create-package.yml`, conditional on a lockfile). The `node`, `python`, `flutter`, `android`, `ios` packs say nothing about CI caching. `static-website` stubs refuse it explicitly so as not to assume a lockfile. The `ci-performance-evaluation` skill profiles tests only; it has no step that asks whether setup and install dominate the run.

Candidate advice, each to be verified against a real run before it is written (basics rule: never document a path not run):
- `node`: `setup-node` with `cache: ${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') != '' && 'npm' || '' }}`, the conditional form chrome-extension already uses; also that setup-node now auto-enables npm caching when `package.json` declares `packageManager`, so a repo without a lockfile must set `package-manager-cache: false` or the step fails. `static-website`'s two stubs could take the same conditional form without adding a config key.
- `python`: `setup-python` `cache: pip` keyed on `requirements*.txt`.
- `android`: `gradle/actions/setup-gradle` caching. `flutter`: the pub cache via the Flutter setup action's cache input. `ios`: SPM / DerivedData caching is contentious; probably a note that it rarely pays.
- `headless-browser`: the existing rule (use the image's browser, never let the driver download) stands; a browser cache is the fallback only where the image lacks the browser.
- `ci-performance-evaluation` skill: a step 0 that reads the setup-versus-work split and sends install-dominated runs to caching rather than to test profiling.
- `git-github-advanced` skill: the three scoping gotchas above (PR-scope writes, low-trust read-only, 7-day eviction), since each silently makes a cache a no-op.

## Decisions for the owner

1. Fix the scheduler's per-task commit re-reads (memo, git-based read, or persisted cache)? Recommendation: the in-run memo first; it removes most of the cost with no workflow change.
2. Author the member-facing caching advice in the tech packs and the two skills?
3. Cache the pinned `npx` downloads in release tasks (needs `cache-mode: write` on the executor job)? {"id":5443277203,"number":2012,"state":"open","locked":false,"title":"GitHub Actions cache: where it helps Claudinite's machinery and members, and where it doesn't","body":"Analysis of the GitHub Actions cache offering against this repo's real run ledger and the pack corpus. No code changed; this issue records the findings and the candidate actions for the owner to pick from.

## The offering, as GitHub documents it today

- `actions/cache` (v6; also `cache/restore` and `cache/save` for split control), and `setup-node` / `setup-python` / `setup-java` / `setup-go` `cache:` inputs that key on a lockfile.
- 10 GB per repository free; entries not accessed for **7 days** are evicted.
- A cache is **branch-scoped**: a run reads its own branch, then the default branch. A cache written by a `pull_request` run lands under `refs/pull/N/merge` and is reusable only by re-runs of that PR. To be useful across branches, a `push` (or `schedule` / `workflow_dispatch`) run on the default branch must write it.
- **Low-trust triggers** (`issues`, `issue_comment`, `workflow_run`, `pull_request_target`, …) get **read-only** access to the default-branch scope unless the job declares `cache-mode: write`. This directly concerns the executor workflow, which is triggered by `issues: labeled`.
- A cache is immutable per key; "updating" means a unique key plus `restore-keys` prefix fallback, which burns quota per run.

## What the canon's own jobs actually spend (run ledger, 2026-09-13)

| Workflow | Total | Setup (checkout + setup-node) | Real work |
|---|---|---|---|
| CI | ~150 s | 11 s (`fetch-depth: 0` checkout 7 s, setup-node 4 s) | unit tests 131 s, sweeps 3 s |
| Scheduler (`scheduler-run`) | ~5 min | 3 s | precondition signal collection ~4 m 40 s, all GitHub API reads |
| Executor (`execute`) | ~20 s | 2 s | queue reads and the Claude Code Remote dispatch, ~15 s |

- The canon has no `package.json`; nothing installs. The runner image already has Node. **A dependency cache has nothing to hold here.**
- Every declared task's `code_work` is `node worker.mjs`; the agentic phase is one HTTP call to Claude Code Remote and the job exits. **The executor job is not where agent time goes**, so a runner cache cannot help the tasks executor's main cost.

## Where the minutes really go: the scheduler's API round-trips

`packs/claudinite-tasks/signals/index.mjs` `windowCommits` does one `/repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}` read per commit in the window, and `collectSignals` is called **per task**, so the same commit is re-read once per task (13 tasks this run; the weekly tasks each saw 40 commits). Hundreds of sequential API calls ≈ 4.5 minutes, and members pay the same shape nightly.

Three fixes, in order of value; only the third is an Actions cache:
1. **In-run memo** of commit-detail reads keyed by sha, shared across tasks. One read per commit per run. Small code change in the signals collector; no cache infra.
2. **Read from git instead of the API**: a `fetch-depth: 0` checkout costs 7 s in CI and `git log --name-only --since` answers the whole window with zero API calls. Changes the scheduler stub's checkout depth, which is workflow content (lands only via a migration record).
3. **Persist the memo across runs** with `actions/cache/restore` + `save` around the run step, keyed on the default-branch sha with a prefix `restore-keys`. The scheduler runs on `schedule` / `workflow_dispatch`, so it may write default-branch caches; the executor (an `issues`-triggered, read-only run) could read the same warmed cache. This is the one shape in which the executor benefits from a cache at all. Cost: 7-day eviction means a weekly-only warmer would lose it; the twice-daily scheduler keeps it warm.

## Other repeated fetches, judged

- `claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/worker.mjs` clones the canon `--depth 1` per member per cycle. The canon's packed objects are a few MB; the clone is seconds. Restoring a cache tarball costs about the same. **Not worth caching.** (The canary workflow does clone the canon twice, once in checkout and once in the worker; a wasted few seconds, not a cache problem.)
- `pack-version-bump` unshallows and `pack-versions.yml` uses `fetch-depth: 0`: 7 s each. Not worth caching.
- `cloudflare-site/tasks/site-release/worker.mjs` runs `npx --yes wrangler@4.128.0` and `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` runs `npx --yes chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3`: a pinned download per release, tens of seconds. Cacheable via `actions/cache` on `~/.npm` keyed on the pinned version, but the executor job is read-only on default scope, so it needs `cache-mode: write` or a warmer. Low value; record as an option.

## Where the value is: advice to members

The corpus has exactly one `cache:` line (`packs/chrome-extension/stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-create-package.yml`, conditional on a lockfile). The `node`, `python`, `flutter`, `android`, `ios` packs say nothing about CI caching. `static-website` stubs refuse it explicitly so as not to assume a lockfile. The `ci-performance-evaluation` skill profiles tests only; it has no step that asks whether setup and install dominate the run.

Candidate advice, each to be verified against a real run before it is written (basics rule: never document a path not run):
- `node`: `setup-node` with `cache: ${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') != '' && 'npm' || '' }}`, the conditional form chrome-extension already uses; also that setup-node now auto-enables npm caching when `package.json` declares `packageManager`, so a repo without a lockfile must set `package-manager-cache: false` or the step fails. `static-website`'s two stubs could take the same conditional form without adding a config key.
- `python`: `setup-python` `cache: pip` keyed on `requirements*.txt`.
- `android`: `gradle/actions/setup-gradle` caching. `flutter`: the pub cache via the Flutter setup action's cache input. `ios`: SPM / DerivedData caching is contentious; probably a note that it rarely pays.
- `headless-browser`: the existing rule (use the image's browser, never let the driver download) stands; a browser cache is the fallback only where the image lacks the browser.
- `ci-performance-evaluation` skill: a step 0 that reads the setup-versus-work split and sends install-dominated runs to caching rather than to test profiling.
- `git-github-advanced` skill: the three scoping gotchas above (PR-scope writes, low-trust read-only, 7-day eviction), since each silently makes a cache a no-op.

## Decisions for the owner

1. Fix the scheduler's per-task commit re-reads (memo, git-based read, or persisted cache)? Recommendation: the in-run memo first; it removes most of the cost with no workflow change.
2. Author the member-facing caching advice in the tech packs and the two skills?
3. Cache the pinned `npx` downloads in release tasks (needs `cache-mode: write` on the executor job)? Recommendation: no, until a release task's duration is a input.body:
Every commit-derived signal collector resolved a window commit's file list with its own API read, and the scheduler collects signals once per task, so one run read the same immutable object once per task that windows on commits. On the 2026-09-13 10:35 scheduler run that was 13 tasks over a 40-commit weekly window: ~4 m 40 s of a 4 m 55 s job on sequential `/commits/{sha}` reads. The `commits` collector also ignored the window the collection had already resolved into `ctx.commits`, doubling its own share.

## What changed

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/signals/index.mjs`: the detail read is memoised per reader for the life of the process, keyed on repo and sha. Only a 200 is kept, so a rate limit or a 5xx is the next collector's to retry rather than the run's verdict. A separate reader (a fleet reader over another repo, a test's fake `gh`) never sees a sha another one resolved. The `commits` collector now reads `ctx.commits` like its siblings.
- `packs/claudinite-tasks/test/signals.test.mjs`: three tests, watched failing first — a second collection reads no commit detail again, a failed read is retried rather than pinned, and two readers never share a sha.

## Verification

Whole suite green locally (3541 tests), `check_the_work` silent. The effect shows in the next scheduled run's `scheduler-run` duration; the run before this change is https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/34752255451 (4 m 55 s).

Closes #2013
